selected_news.title: Feridun Sinirlioğlu, Türkiye’nin UN Sekreterliği Adayı
selected_news.summary: Turkish candidate for top UN post reflects Ankara’s reform ambition | Daily Sabah Daily Sabah
selected_news.source_headline: Turkish candidate for top UN post reflects Ankara’s reform ambition
selected_news.article_text: On Friday, Feridun Sinirlioğlu was scheduled to be interviewed by the United Nations in a broadcast session called “interactive dialogue,” as the international body seeks its next secretary-general, a prestigious job a Turkish national has never been nominated for before. His vision statement, presented to the U.N. as part of his application to the post, lays out his aspiration to uphold the body’s mission for global peace. Experts say this aligns well with Türkiye’s advocacy for a fairer world where the U.N. represents more than a bunch of major powers. The 70-year-old diplomat is no stranger to the atmosphere, with a career that began at the Turkish Foreign Ministry in the 1980s and took him from Kenya to New York over decades. The former foreign minister worked as Türkiye’s representative at the United Nations between 2016 and 2023 and as a U.N. Special Coordinator on Afghanistan. He currently serves as secretary-general of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE). He seems like the perfect candidate for Türkiye, which has raised its diplomatic profile in the past two decades as an influential actor in global affairs. Professor Nurşin Ateşoğlu Güney of the National Intelligence Academy (MIA), a member of the Presidential Security and Foreign Policy Council, says Sinirlioğlu is “a highly experienced and respected diplomat with an extensive network in international relations.” Merve Suna Özel Özcan, associate professor and the vice chair of the International Relations Department at Kırıkkale University, says Sinirlioğlu’s nomination is “an institutional and diplomatic manifestation of President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's longstanding principle that 'the world is bigger than five.’” Erdoğan invokes this motto in almost all U.N.-related speeches, referring to the five members of the U.N. Security Council and how they shape current events, leaving little room for other countries. “This nomination carries significance far beyond the candidacy of a Turkish diplomat for one of the highest positions in the international system. It reflects an attempt to translate Türkiye's longstanding criticism of the existing international order into a willingness to assume greater institutional responsibility,” Özcan told Daily Sabah. “For the past 15 years, Türkiye has been among the countries most openly calling for reform of the United Nations in terms of its structure, functions and scope, under the leadership of our president. Against this backdrop, I believe Türkiye’s candidate already stands apart from the other candidates. Indeed, when we look at the vision statement of Mr. Sinirlioğlu, we see important messages that distinguish him from the others, particularly his emphasis on the need for the United Nations to become much more effective, return to its founding principles and embrace reform,” Şuay Nilhan Açıkalın, associate professor at the International Relations Department of Ankara Hacı Bayram Veli University, said. “International peace and security are under unprecedented strain. War is ravaging peoples and lands across the globe; widening economic inequalities undermine the legitimate aspiration of future generations to achieve greater prosperity than those who came before them; demographic shifts and global migration patterns raise new challenges that demand coordinated international responses; human rights are violated in plain sight and weakened by intolerable double standards; and transnational threats, including organized crime and terrorism, challenge states’ sovereignty and threaten the security of all. At the same time, a new technological revolution is unfolding, generating both extraordinary opportunities and profound uncertainty,” Sinirlioğlu said in his vision statement presented to the United Nations. Özcan noted that Erdoğan’s “the world is bigger than five” principle “should not be understood merely as criticism directed at the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council.” “It represents a broader questioning of the international system's structural problems of representation, justice and legitimacy. The growing discrepancy between the institutional order established after World War II and today's increasingly complex distribution of global power has become more evident. In particular, the deadlocks experienced within the Security Council in responding to crises such as Gaza and the Russia-Ukraine war have exposed serious limitations in the United Nations' ability to maintain international peace and security,” she said. Conflicts have escalated throughout the past decade and linger to this day, in one way or another, continuing to test the U.N.’s effectiveness in thwarting them as the world edges closer to World War III at times and mobilizes for peace during respites from raging tensions, as was seen during the Russia-Ukraine conflict and in response to Israel’s atrocities that have claimed the lives of tens of thousands of Palestinians since 2023. Yeliz Albayrak, a lecturer at Istanbul Aydın University and a political science and international relations expert, said the changes Türkiye called for at the United Nations “essentially reflect the recognition that the system established after World War II, particularly the overarching institution designed to regulate the entire international system, has proved inadequate.” “I believe Sinirlioğlu's nomination should be understood as Türkiye's diplomatic response to the United Nations' growing crisis of institutional effectiveness. Türkiye is not simply identifying the shortcomings of the existing international system. It is also expressing an aspiration to assume greater responsibility in efforts to make that system more inclusive, equitable and effective. In other words, we are witnessing an attempt to transform a longstanding critique of the international order into a concrete diplomatic initiative,” Özcan stated. “The timing of the nomination should also be considered within this broader framework. Although its announcement at a relatively late stage is noteworthy, appointments to senior positions in international organizations are shaped not only by individual qualifications but also by multilateral negotiations and the dynamics of consensus among major powers. Sinirlioğlu's experience as Türkiye's foreign minister, permanent representative to the United Nations and secretary-general of the OSCE is particularly relevant in this context. Nevertheless, the position of United Nations secretary-general does not serve to represent the foreign policy priorities of any individual country. The broader international legitimacy of this candidacy will therefore depend on its ability to secure the confidence of different member states and demonstrate a genuinely independent commitment to multilateralism. I also associate this development with Türkiye's approach to stability diplomacy. What the international system requires today is not merely a United Nations capable of responding to crises after they emerge, but an institution capable of preventing escalation, maintaining dialogue between conflicting parties and contributing to sustainable international stability. Ultimately, Sinirlioğlu's nomination represents an attempt to translate the systemic criticism embodied in the principle that 'the world is bigger than five' into an aspiration for greater participation and responsibility in shaping the future of international institutions. What I find particularly significant is that Türkiye is not merely arguing that the international system must change; it is also seeking to take part, at the institutional level, in that process,” Özcan said. “In this respect, the candidacy is quite critical. Of course, the candidacy processes at the United Nations are important for every country, both in terms of lobbying and diplomatic efforts. It is worth noting that securing this position is particularly significant for the candidate’s home country, regardless of which country they represent. "In recent years, Türkiye has clearly emerged as one of the few countries making significant contributions to regional and global peace and stability through international diplomacy. Both its mediation efforts and its humanitarian aid policy, which places it among the world's leading countries in this field, have made Türkiye a country held up as an example. Considering almost all the conflicts currently taking place around the world, we can say that Türkiye has adopted a much more active approach to these conflict situations. Perhaps it is worth sincerely emphasizing once again just how significant a message Türkiye's decision to field a candidate for the United Nations sends. Türkiye attaches importance to the U.N. returning to its founding principles through a reform-oriented approach. As our president has put it, this is a particularly important candidacy and process in terms of ensuring that the United Nations, as an international organization, plays an effective role within the international system and contributes to building a fairer and more equitable world,” Açıkalın said. “(Sinirlioğlu’s candidacy) is also directly linked to Ankara’s recognition as a respected and influential middle power in its region. Considering Ankara’s diplomatic engagement and influence both in its region and beyond, we can say that Sinirlioğlu is a highly suitable candidate, given his own expertise and experience,” Güney said. “The issue of U.N. reform is an important matter that has been repeatedly raised by Türkiye’s president. At a time when serious conflicts are unfolding across the international arena, the U.N. Security Council frequently finds itself deadlocked. This is largely due to the failure to implement the reforms the council needs. Reform is essential to ensuring world peace and enabling the organization to play an effective role in this regard,” Güney said. "Although some have described Türkiye's decision to nominate a candidate as late or a last-minute move, there were, of course, certain processes that had to be taken into consideration. "We know that there was an expectation for a candidate from Latin America, as candidates are selected from different regions on a rotational basis. There may have been a waiting period out of respect for this arrangement. However, since no consensus had emerged around a candidate and the end of the five-year term (of Guterres) was approaching, Türkiye put forward a candidate who had previously received broad support and had been endorsed by a large number of countries, including many that are currently at war with one another, through OSCE,” Albayrak said. “This candidate had already brought these countries together through their joint support for his candidacy. We know that the OSCE has also played a diplomatic role in resolving disputes. It is not a military organization or a defense pact, nor is it an economic bloc; it is an organization for cooperation. In fact, we could describe it as the largest umbrella organization bringing together these states, including countries currently experiencing serious disputes and conflicts. Sinirlioğlu was a candidate jointly selected by countries across this broad spectrum, including Russia, nuclear powers and states involved in crises and wars. Seeking to appoint someone with such an extensive level of international backing to a position at the United Nations is particularly significant. His candidacy carries a much higher degree of acceptance and offers greater potential for cooperation,” Albayrak added. Sinirlioğlu was in Belarus earlier this week as OSCE secretary-general and met President Aleksandr Lukashenko, as well as visiting Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, in the first such visit by an OSCE chief since 2019. Türkiye is one of the founding members of the United Nations. It joined the body in 1945 shortly after signing the U.N. Charter. selected_news.title: Demokratların zaferi sonrası borsalar endişe içinde
selected_news.summary: Asian and European markets follow US tech rout with many analysts predicting more waves of selling to come European and Asian stock markets fell sharply on Friday after the Democrats’ decisive victory in the midterms triggered a rout in US tech stocks a day earlier. A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stock markets on Friday. The investor sentiment then reached London, where the market was, at one stage, poised for its worst day since March. Continue reading...
selected_news.source_headline: Global stocks fall amid ‘big worries over AI’ after Democrats’ midterms triumph
selected_news.article_text: Asian and European markets follow US tech rout with many analysts predicting more waves of selling to come European and Asian stock markets fell sharply on Friday after the Democrats’ decisive victory in the midterms triggered a rout in US tech stocks a day earlier A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stock markets on Friday. The investor sentiment then reached London, where the market was, at one stage, poised for its worst day since March The FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, was down as much as 254 points, or 2.35%, at 10,528 points during a wave of selling in morning trading. But by the close of the day it had clawed back some of its losses to be down 1%, helped by a rise in US stocks when Wall Street reopened Germany’s Dax index fell by 2%, France’s Cac 40 dropped by 0.8% and Spain’s Ibex lost 0.6% Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe “Big worries are colliding – the build-out of datacentres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment.” However, there were signs of easing jitters on Wall Street on Friday, where tech stocks rose, lifting the S&P 500 share index by 0.3% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq closed up 1% – which only recovered a portion of their previous day’s losses That followed a stronger-than-expected employment report that showed the US economy added 165,000 new jobs in October, pulling the unemployment rate down to 4.1% On Thursday, the Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5% Chip stocks led the slump on Thursday, with the memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 22% and the hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 17%. Wall Street’s “fear index”, the Vix, jumped by more than 60% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility The heavy falls continued in Asia on Friday, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 index sinking 6% and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbling more than 6.5% “It’s actually a bit of a disaster,” said Christopher Forbes, the head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets “[Clients] were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out. All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints … because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome, and you’re telling them: ‘Look, you’ve just lost money.’” Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “Yesterday’s [Thursday’s] brutal session marked a dramatic turnaround from Wednesday, but with AI fears still prominent there is a risk that there is much more selling to come “Investors remain on watch for a potential resumption of the Iran conflict, and are nervously watching the oil price after its slump earlier in the week. All in all it remains a very febrile atmosphere.” However, despite the sharp losses suffered on global stock markets around the world, most indices are still up for the year. The Nasdaq Composite index remains up 6.35% since the start of January – even though it is more than 10% below its peak The FTSE 100 has gained almost 7.5% in 2026 – but it is now more than 300 points below the record high set in July Mohit Kumar, an economist at the investment bank Jefferies, said that while he did not expect a quick rebound from Thursday’s losses in the US, he also did not believe it marked the “start of the unwind of the AI trade” He said: “AI investment has been a key driver of US growth and we do not see the Democrats as giving up on this growth engine. Datacentres and AI infrastructure also create jobs and Democrats would be reluctant to let those jobs move on to other states or outside the country.” Stock market tremors have also hit the London Metal Exchange, with copper poised for its biggest weekly fall since March Benchmark three-month copper, a key metal used in the semiconductor, electronics and automotive industry, has dropped 0.61%, leaving it positioned for a 2.79% fall this week Craig Lang, a principal analyst at the consultancy CRU, said the price of copper was increasingly influenced by the AI market and “sentiment towards datacentre expansion”
